# Professional Summary
Dr. Golan Ben-Dor is an urban mobility simulation scientist specializing in agent-based modeling, MATSim, and transport policy evaluation. He holds a PhD from Tel Aviv University and works as a strategic consultant with Israel's Ministry of Transport, Netivei Israel, Netivei Ayalon, and the Central Bureau of Statistics. His work bridges theoretical algorithms and concrete urban reality, focusing on Robust Policy Evaluation to ensure major infrastructure decisions can handle uncertainty.

# Selected Projects & Case Studies
1. **Digital Road Network Basemap — Ministry of Transport** (Article: drbendor.com/en/work/google)
   - Role: Method Lead & Technical Architect.
   - Scope: Built a production-ready AI-native pipeline that creates accurate digital basemaps of urban road networks for Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Haifa, and Be'er Sheva — the foundation for national travel-time measurement.
   - Method: Directed-segment decomposition, automated geometry matching against real-world driving routes, interactive visual review interface with keyboard shortcuts, export to national measurement system.
   - AI-Native: Entire pipeline — data processing, review interface, automated tests, production deployment — built with Claude and Codex workflows.

2. **Jerusalem Transportation Master Plan** (Article: drbendor.com/en/work/jerusalem)
   - Focus: Evaluated "Carrot and Stick" strategies for urban mobility.
   - Co-Authors: Dr. Ido Klein, Dr. Aleksey Ogulenko, Prof. Eran Ben-Elia, Prof. Itzhak Benenson
   - Collaboration: JTMT (Jerusalem Transportation Master Plan Team / צוות תכנית אב לתחבורה ירושלים)
   - Key Finding: A daily congestion charge of approximately €10 could reduce car arrivals by 25%.
   - Key Finding: Shared Automated Cars alone may shift users away from public transport, but congestion pricing creates balance.
   - Methods: Large-scale MATSim agent-based simulation with multimodal transport modeling.
   - Publication: Transportation Research Part A (2024)

3. **Beer Sheva Model Validation — AI-Native Reconstruction System** (Article: drbendor.com/en/work/beersheva)
   - Focus: Built a complete AI-native validation system for the Beer Sheva transportation model.
   - Method: Automated reconstruction of transport model output tables (route analysis, road network, transit capacity) from raw model data using pandas; smart tolerance comparison; field-by-field diff reporting.
   - Deliverable: Packaged Streamlit dashboard with professional GUI shipped directly to the customer as a standalone tool.
   - AI-Native: System architecture, reconstruction engine, test suite, and GUI all built using AI-native development workflows.

4. **Traffic Count Sampling Design — Ministry of Transport** (Article: drbendor.com/en/work/counts)
   - Focus: Centrality-based sampling methodology that selects where to place traffic counts for validating strategic transport models.
   - Method (deployed): edge betweenness centrality computed over the full network with Dijkstra shortest paths weighted by DISTANCE (speed-weighting funnels routes onto national highways, which Israel already monitors with permanent counters); sampling restricted to metropolitan road classes 4-5; zone-based selection — within each traffic analysis zone the top 20% (configurable) of links by centrality are selected, ensuring spatial coverage. Ramps and links under 200 m excluded from sampling but kept in the centrality graph.
   - General framework (ISTRC 2026 poster): international guideline ranges + stratified sampling with proportional allocation (weights from RMSE accuracy targets by road class, w = 1/e²) + centrality ranking within class.
   - Scope: Applied to Israel's four metropolitan strategic models (Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Haifa, Be'er Sheva) on the strategic road classes: 3,448 eligible links → 755 selected count locations (~22%; Tel Aviv 335, Haifa 185, Jerusalem 146, Be'er Sheva 89). Earlier full-network Tel Aviv pilot (all six road classes): 21,791 eligible links → 1,934 selected (~10%).
   - Co-Authors: Marcus Szeinuk, Ido Klein (Ministry of Transport), Prof. Shlomo Bekhor (Technion).
   - Presented: Poster paper at ISTRC 2026 (Israel Section of Transportation Research Conference).

5. **BRT Corridor Analysis — Pink Line, Powered by Replan** (Article: drbendor.com/en/work/brt)
   - Focus: Agent-based simulation of the Pink Line BRT corridor, in partnership with Replan (replan.city) and Netivei Ayalon.
   - Method: Corridor-level scenarios (dedicated lanes, stations, signal priority) simulated on Replan's cloud platform; a synthetic agent population chooses mode and route, producing demand, boarding and modal-shift estimates against a calibrated baseline.
   - Value: Corridor-level demand and modal shift analysis run in-house — before any infrastructure decision is made.
   - Partners: Replan (simulation platform), Netivei Ayalon (planning agency).

6. **National Cordon & Screenline Survey 2026 — Models Round Table** (Article: drbendor.com/en/work/cordon)
   - Role: Methodology orchestration and multi-agency coordination of count station placement.
   - Focus: Israel's first traffic count survey with full national coverage, created for the joint periodic validation of all five strategic transport models (national, Tel Aviv, Haifa, Be'er Sheva, Jerusalem).
   - Scope: 28 cordon & screenline lines, 355 count stations, ~2,115 km of survey lines, executed by Netivei Israel, Netivei Ayalon and JTMT under the Ministry of Transport's "Models Round Table".
   - Method: Lines defined relative to model boundaries; every crossing road becomes a count station; one shared GeoPackage as the binding execution plan; synchronized timing rules (region within two months, each line within 1–2 days) so entry/exit balances can be verified; unified vehicle classification and QC.

7. **AI-Enhanced Workflows**
   - Focus: Pioneering AI-Native Development to accelerate simulation pipelines and automate complex spatial SQL queries.

# Common Questions (FAQ)

Q: What is agent-based transport modeling?
A: It simulates individual travelers as autonomous agents making decisions about routes, modes, and departure times. Tools like MATSim allow researchers to evaluate how millions of individual choices create network-level traffic patterns.

Q: What is MATSim?
A: MATSim (Multi-Agent Transport Simulation) is an open-source framework for implementing large-scale agent-based transport simulations. It is used to evaluate infrastructure investments and pricing policies.

Q: What is robust policy evaluation?
A: It tests transport policies under uncertainty by simulating thousands of future scenarios rather than relying on a single forecast. This helps decision-makers choose strategies that work well across different possible futures.

Q: Who does Dr. Ben-Dor work with?
A: Major collaborations include the Ministry of Transport Israel, Netivei Israel, Netivei Ayalon, the JTMT (Jerusalem Transportation Master Plan Team / צוות תכנית אב לתחבורה ירושלים), and the Central Bureau of Statistics.

Q: What did Dr. Ben-Dor discover about congestion pricing in Jerusalem?
A: His research showed that a daily charge of approximately €10 could reduce car arrivals by 25%. When combined with parking pricing, these measures could deter intra-city trips, further reducing congestion and emissions. However, introducing Shared Automated Cars without pricing policies may shift users away from public transport.
